items.meaning_mnemonic: On the farm only the <radical>cow</radical> gets a real name, so every other object that is <radical>not</radical> her is written off as a plain <kanji>thing</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Boots</reading> the sulky mailman kicks every loose <kanji>thing</kanji> off the path and spits 「<reading>ぶつ</reading>」 at each one he sends flying.

items.meaning_mnemonic: When you quit cooking <radical>food (left)</radical> and do the exact <radical>opposite</radical>, you finally sit down to a proper <kanji>meal</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <kanji>meal</kanji> from <reading>Han</reading> always turns up sliced straight down the middle, because he cannot say 「<reading>はん</reading>」 without halving whatever sits on your plate.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fish</kanji> is the only animal that will <radical>crouch</radical> in a flooded <radical>rice field</radical> until the water is gone and the <radical>fire</radical> is licking the bottom of the pan.
items.reading_mnemonic: A rockhound crouched at the riverbank is splitting open a <reading>geode</reading> when a fat carp launches out of the shallows and slaps her flat across the face. She topples backward with a startled <reading>ぎょ</reading>, and the fish flops calmly back in as if nothing happened.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a steaming cup: delicate <radical>grass</radical> leaves curling up top like visible steam, a little <radical>person</radical> warming his hands round a <radical>tree</radical>-carved cup below. That curling steam over the cup is the whole picture: <kanji>tea</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A dance instructor spins through the tearoom mid cha-cha lesson, a full teacup balanced on his palm. He counts the beat out loud — 「<reading>ちゃ</reading>」-cha-cha — until the cup tips and the lesson ends the same soaked way every time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>ill</kanji> body is just a healthy one that <radical>sickness</radical> has bumped down to <radical>third class</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A mangy owl called <reading>Bee-Owl</reading> is so <kanji>ill</kanji> it can no longer hoot, and every 「<reading>びょう</reading>」 it coughs up costs it another feather.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Raise a truly <radical>perfect</radical> hall high on its own <radical>hill (left)</radical>, and it is grand enough to be called an <kanji>Inst.</kanji>
items.reading_mnemonic: The keeper of the world's biggest <reading>inn</reading> keeps adding wings and halls, yet still bellows 「<reading>いん</reading>」 across a courtyard that has swollen into a full <kanji>Inst.</kanji>
items.description: Short for institution: it names big establishments such as hospitals, temples, and government bodies, and rarely stands alone.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Any <kanji>building</kanji> is just an empty shell until a <radical>bureaucrat</radical> moves in with his stamp and there is enough <radical>food (left)</radical> over from lunch to keep him at the desk.
items.reading_mnemonic: The night caretaker <reading>Khan</reading> looks after exactly one <kanji>building</kanji>, and he snaps 「<reading>かん</reading>」 at anyone who so much as leans on its door after closing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cave</radical> that a whole <radical>construction</radical> crew has finished digging out is, for all that effort, still just an <kanji>empty</kanji> hollow in the hill.
items.reading_mnemonic: The pigeon <reading>Coo</reading> will only settle somewhere <kanji>empty</kanji>, because he needs the bare walls to bounce his proud 「<reading>くう</reading>」 back at him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: One line dragged over flat <radical>ground</radical> is just a mark until an <radical>open box</radical> frames it, which is the entire <radical>reason</radical> it now reads as a deliberate <kanji>brush-stroke</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The painter <reading>Gar</reading> grunts 「<reading>が</reading>」 on every single <kanji>brush-stroke</kanji>, so a busy afternoon of work leaves him too hoarse to speak.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>roof</kanji> is nothing but a sagging <radical>body</radical> sprawled overhead, and you only notice it the moment you <radical>arrive</radical> under it out of the rain.
items.reading_mnemonic: The carpenter <reading>Oak</reading> turns down every job except a <kanji>roof</kanji>, and he barks 「<reading>おく</reading>」 down at you from the ridge beam the whole time he nails it on.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 台 as a squat stone pedestal: a <radical>cocoon</radical>-shaped knob on top, over a wide <radical>mouth</radical> of a base bolted to the ground. Workers winch a bronze statue onto it, and the block doesn't budge under the weight: solid, built for holding something up — a <kanji>pedestal</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Dai</reading>, the giant baby, climbs onto that same pedestal to pose like a statue. One stomp cracks the stone with a boom that rattles windows, and he wails <reading>だい</reading>, <reading>だい</reading> as the block crumbles beneath him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 番 as a ticket dispenser bolted to a wall, its slots ruled like a tiny <radical>rice field</radical>, spitting out numbered slips kept strictly <radical>separate</radical>. Customers file into line by number, nobody out of place: the pure order of your <kanji>turn</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a guard named <reading>Ban</reading> slams a wooden stamp onto the counter each time a new number is called. The crack echoes <reading>ばん</reading> through the shop as the line shuffles forward, one turn at a time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Paper</kanji> is a mat of <radical>thread</radical> pulp beaten flat until it can hold a <radical>family name</radical> stamped on it in one clean press.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi's clerk <reading>Sheila</reading> won't touch plastic and wraps every sale in <kanji>paper</kanji>, hissing 「<reading>し</reading>」 with each sheet she tears off the roll.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Something is <kanji>true</kanji> only when all <radical>ten</radical> inspectors, each checking with the same steady <radical>tool</radical>, come back with the same answer.
items.reading_mnemonic: A courtroom lie-detector nicknamed <reading>Shin</reading> chimes <reading>しん</reading> the moment a statement is <kanji>true</kanji>, so nervous witnesses keep over-explaining just to hear it side with them.
items.description: Besides 'true', this kanji often acts as a prefix meaning 'dead-' or 'exactly': dead centre, right in the middle, pure white. In that spot it means 'completely', not 'true'.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Take a <radical>sword</radical> to a single carrot <radical>seven</radical> times and what is left on the board is past chopped, past sliced, just plain <kanji>cut</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The girls' final at the school drags into <reading>set two</reading>, and the deciding rally ends when a racket string snaps and has to be cut clean before anyone can serve. The umpire trims it with scissors, muttering <reading>せつ</reading>, and flicks the loose ends off the court.
items.description: Beyond literal cutting, this kanji also means doing something keenly or intensely, which is why it sits inside common words for 'important' and 'kind.'

items.meaning_mnemonic: Any breeze that counts as <kanji>wind</kanji> is one clean <radical>slash</radical> of air strong enough to lift an <radical>insect</radical> off the picnic <radical>table</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the same picnic table, the insect finally wins, so Hank pushes his half-eaten <reading>food</reading> away and lets out one long, tired sigh, <reading>ふう</reading>. With every breath out, the wind grabs another napkin off the table. He gives up and watches his lunch scatter across the grass.
items.description: Besides moving air, 風 has a second common sense: style or manner, the way something looks or is done. It turns up in words that contrast traditional and modern style, where it means roughly in the manner of.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing <radical>heavy</radical> will <kanji>move</kanji> even a single inch until you shove a burst of raw <radical>power</radical> in behind it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Lazy baker <reading>Dough</reading> won't stir by hand, so he barks 「<reading>どう</reading>」 at the mixer until the blades start to <kanji>move</kanji> on their own.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Beads of <radical>white</radical> <radical>ice</radical> strung along the branches of a bare <radical>tree</radical> knock together in the wind and shiver into faint <kanji>music</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a tone-deaf monk named <reading>Gawk</reading> whacks the giant bell and howls 「<reading>がく</reading>」, and the cats bolt from what he calls <kanji>music</kanji>.
items.description: This character also means comfortable, easy, or fun, not only music, and it switches to a different on'yomi in that everyday sense.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 近 as a signpost arrow, chopped short by an <radical>axe</radical>, that curled back along the <radical>road</radical> to jab at your own boots. On the mountain trail, the vending machine you swore was another hour up turns out one switchback away: <kanji>near</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At that vending machine, the hiker's little brother — pure <reading>kin</reading>, tagging along everywhere — presses his face to the glass and chants the machine's name like a drumbeat: <reading>きん</reading>. He is always, always this close.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>walk</kanji> is slow travel where your feet <radical>stop</radical> flat on the ground so often that you cover only a <radical>few</radical> steps a minute.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the steep mountain trail, Grandma Kane climbs one slow step at a time, leaning her full weight on an old garden <reading>hoe</reading> and grunting <reading>ほ</reading> each time a foot lands flat. At this rate the vending machine at the top is an hour off, but she plants the hoe and takes the next step anyway.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 勉 as a sweatband wrung out mid-cram with sheer <radical>power</radical>, soaking the page underneath. In Koichi's konbini, a student camped by the onigiri shelf pulls an all-nighter, refusing to be <radical>exempt</radical>, wringing the band out again and again: pure <kanji>exertion</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk ringing up onigiri all night, <reading>Ben</reading>, groans the same sympathetic <reading>べん</reading> every time the sweatband hits the counter, cheering the cramming on until the beeping till finally goes quiet.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who plants himself in a house long enough to be treated as its <radical>lord</radical> has done nothing but <kanji>dwell</kanji> there.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Jude</reading> has not stepped outside his flat in ten years, and when the landlord knocks he just groans 「<reading>じゅう</reading>」 and goes on <kanji>dwell</kanji>ing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 問 as a <radical>gate</radical> with a <radical>mouth</radical> built into the crossbar, shouting through the bars at Sei's school. A latecomer rattles the locked gate, and the mouth shouts back, demanding to know why they're late. Nobody gets in without answering the gate's <kanji>question</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Outside that same gate, Mon-Bun — the scholarly rabbit twins — bicker without pause, blaming each other for muddling the question. They let out one long identical <reading>moan</reading> that comes out as <reading>もん</reading>, echoing off the bars, and they're still moaning it when the gate creaks open.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> up front and a second <radical>person</radical> behind, both walking after an angled <radical>chevron</radical> banner in whatever <radical>direction</radical> the signpost's arm points, are on a <kanji>trip</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tour guide called <reading>Rio</reading> begins every <kanji>trip</kanji> by barking 「<reading>りょ</reading>」 the instant the bus doors hiss shut, leaving latecomers to chase the bumper down the road.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who trails a step behind a <radical>samurai</radical> all day, carrying his sandals and his tea, is there to <kanji>attend</kanji> him.
items.reading_mnemonic: A servant called <reading>Sheila</reading> is so keen to <kanji>attend</kanji> her lord that she blurts 「<reading>し</reading>」 the second he clears his throat, already halfway to the kitchen.
items.description: Attend here means waiting on a master, not being present somewhere. In most compounds the character simply means doing or how a thing is done.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>topic</kanji> is the single <radical>right</radical> word that has to sit in a chapter's <radical>head</radical>ing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The truck-sized baby <reading>Dai</reading> finds every family <kanji>topic</kanji> boring unless it is about him, so he bellows his own name, 「<reading>だい</reading>」, until the table gives in and talks about him.
items.description: Beyond topic, this is the ordinary character for the title of a book or film and for an exam or homework question. All three senses share one idea: what the thing is about.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>sound</kanji> is anything that makes you <radical>stand</radical> straight up, alert, in the middle of an otherwise silent <radical>day</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hoarder called Owen is certain every <kanji>sound</kanji> is his to <reading>own</reading>, so he seals each one in a jar marked <reading>おん</reading> and shelves it beside the thunder he caught last week.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Grass</radical> brewed until it plays gentle <radical>music</radical> through every sore joint is the oldest kind of <kanji>medicine</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hand a <kanji>medicine</kanji> spoon to a <reading>yak</reading> and it bellows 「<reading>やく</reading>」 and sprays the syrup straight back at you, because no yak has ever swallowed a thing the vet ordered.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>vehicle</radical> parked on a <radical>cloud</radical> finds nothing to grip, so its wheels just <kanji>revolve</kanji> and it stays put.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ten the circus bear sprints on a rolling log, spinning it under his paws while he stays in one spot, and the ringmaster shouts 「<reading>てん</reading>」, a perfect <reading>ten</reading>, every time the log <kanji>revolve</kanji>s once more.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>sentence</kanji> is a row of words <radical>mow</radical>n short and then capped with a <radical>lid</radical> at the full stop.
items.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the rabbit twins, never get through a single <kanji>sentence</kanji> out loud, because halfway in they both yelp 「<reading>ぶん</reading>」 and lunge for the same sticky <reading>bun</reading>.
items.description: The taught gloss is sentence, but in compounds this character usually widens to writing or culture in general, as in the words for literature, composition, and civilisation.
